title: Worker QThreads are never cleared; the last reference is dropped while running
body:
**File:** `src/gui/tabs/optimization_tab.py:653`; `src/gui/tabs/tolerancing_tab.py:542, 573`

`self._opt_worker` / `self._mc_worker` are assigned and never set back to `None` on completion,
retaining the `OptimizationResult` (a deep copy of the whole optical system) for the tab's lifetime.
This is also the mechanism behind T-08's core dump.

**Fix:** set `self._opt_worker = None` at the top of `_on_optimization_finished` /
`_on_optimization_failed` (after `wait()`), and consider `deleteLater()` on the thread.

nodes.title: fix(gui): release tolerancing workers so results are not retained
nodes.body:
Closes #334

## Problem

Both the Monte Carlo and inverse-sensitivity workers hand back a payload holding a **deep copy of the whole optical system**, and `_mc_worker`/`_inv_worker` were assigned and never set back to `None`. Holding the last Python reference to a finished worker therefore kept that payload alive for the tab's lifetime — one retained deep copy per analysis run, and the same mechanism behind the earlier optimization-tab core dump (T-08).

The optimization half of this ticket was already fixed by that work (`OptimizationTab._release_finished_worker`, called from both completion slots), so this ports the same pattern to the tolerancing tab. Both attributes are now also initialized to `None` — they were previously never set before their first run, so any early read raised `AttributeError`.

## One deliberate difference from the optimization tab

The release is conservative for the same reason: these slots run on the GUI thread while the worker may still be returning from `run()`, and dropping a live QThread's last reference makes CPython destroy it — `~QThread` aborts the process.

But here the release sits in the **middle of a report-rendering handler**, so an exception while querying thread state would cost the user their results. The `isRunning()` check is therefore guarded, and an inconclusive answer keeps the reference — which is what the docstring already promised.

## Verified end to end

```
while running:     _mc_worker = MonteCarloWorker running = True
after completion:  _mc_worker = None
report shown:      '=== MONTE CARLO RESULTS ===\n\nTotal Trials: 10...'
```

## Tests

11 tests, **9 fail without the change**: the release decision in both directions, a live worker blocking its own release, one worker's release not being blocked by another's, both handler slots, and the handler still rendering its report when thread state is unqueryable.

Also updates one assertion in `tests/test_tolerancing_tab.py` that checked for the *absence of the slot* rather than for the absence of a live thread — the slot is now legitimately present and `None`.

title: 3D `_intersect_sphere` accepts a zero-length hit; the 2D guard was never ported
body:
**File:** `src/tracer_3d.py:171` vs `src/tracer_2d.py:187`

```python
# 3D
valid_ts = [t for t in [t1, t2] if t > -EPSILON]      # <- 2D uses t > EPSILON
is_inside = dist_sq < radius**2                       # <- no EPSILON slack
```

The 2D tracer's comment documents this exact defect as already fixed; the fix was never applied to
the 3D copy. If the origin lies exactly on the sphere, `t = 0` is returned, the tracer appends a
duplicate path point with 0 OPL, and refracts the ray in place.

**Fix:** use `t > EPSILON` in the 3D tracer and add the same `radius*radius - EPSILON` slack.

nodes.title: fix(tracer3d): do not record a zero-length hit as a path point
nodes.body:
Closes #335

## I did not apply the fix as written, because it would break cemented doublets

The issue asks the 3D tracer to reject `t ~ 0` the way the 2D tracer does. But `rank_cap_roots` documents that divergence as **deliberate**:

> Callers own this because they disagree on purpose: … the 3D tracer accepts one so that touching surfaces in a cemented doublet still refract.

It is right. When two elements share a vertex, the ray has to change index at the point it is already standing on. Rejecting the hit would stop doublets refracting at the cemented interface.

## What was actually wrong: the recording, not the acceptance

Three sites appended the intersection unconditionally, so a cemented doublet produced **three pairs of consecutive identical path points**:

```
2: x=8.000000  seg=8.000e+00
3: x=8.000000  seg=0.000e+00   <- duplicate
4: x=8.000000  seg=0.000e+00   <- duplicate
5: x=14.000000 seg=6.000e+00
6: x=14.000000 seg=0.000e+00   <- duplicate
```

Anything deriving a direction or a segment length from consecutive path points divides by zero on those. `ray.origin` is still updated, so the refraction is untouched.

The sites: the surface intersection in `tracer_3d`, the aperture-stop append, and `Ray3D.propagate` with a zero distance.

## Verified

```
path points: 5 | duplicates: 0
x positions: [-50, 0.0, 8.0, 14.0, 64.0]
OPL: 122.814400     (unchanged)
```

The cemented vertex at `x = 8` is recorded exactly once. A spaced doublet, an off-axis ray, and the 2D tracer are all unaffected.

## Tests

15 tests, **6 fail without the change**.

title: `image_simulator` reads aberration keys that do not exist and uses Seidel coefficients as pixel σ
body:
**File:** `src/image_simulator.py:172-190`

```python
if "spherical" in aberrations:              # actual key is "spherical_aberration"
    sigma = coeff * 2.0
    result = gaussian_filter(result, sigma=sigma)
if "astigmatism" in aberrations:
    result = gaussian_filter1d(result, sigma=coeff * 2, axis=0)
```

Two problems: (a) `calculate_all_aberrations()` returns `spherical_aberration` (see `optimizer.py:119`),
not `spherical`, so the spherical term never fires; (b) a Seidel coefficient in waves/µm is fed to
`gaussian_filter(sigma=...)`, whose unit is **pixels** — the blur is completely independent of
`pixel_pitch_mm`, and `coeff * 2.0` is an unexplained magic scale. The astigmatism term applies a 1-D
blur and leaves the orthogonal axis untouched (rank-deficient).

**Fix:** convert the wavefront coefficient to a length at the image plane, divide by
`pixel_pitch_mm`, use `max(0.0, ...)` (not `if coeff > 0`), and match the real key names.

nodes.title: fix(image_sim): scale aberration blur by the pixel pitch
nodes.body:
Closes #336

## Problem

`_apply_aberrations` took the Seidel values from `calculate_all_aberrations` — which are geometric, **in millimetres** — and passed them straight to `gaussian_filter`'s `sigma`, whose unit is **pixels**:

```python
sigma = coeff * 2.0
```

So the aberration blur was **completely independent of `pixel_pitch_mm`** — the identical image at any sensor pitch came out identically blurred — and the `* 2.0` was an unexplained magic scale. For a 5.38 mm spherical aberration at 0.01 mm pitch the correct σ is ~538 px; the old code produced **10.8**.

## Fix

Each term is converted to millimetres at the image plane, then to pixels with the real pitch — the same conversion `_apply_diffraction` already uses for the Airy disk, so the two effects finally share one scale:

```
0.05 mm coefficient ->  sigma 2.5 / 5 / 10 px  at  0.02 / 0.01 / 0.005 mm pitch
peak height falls as 1/sigma^2, as it must
```

**Key names** are now read defensively. The code asked for `"spherical"` while the calculator's canonical name is `"spherical_aberration"`. Both documented aliases exist today, so either is accepted rather than assuming one — the failure mode in the report was a term that silently never fires.

`if coeff > 0` became `max(0.0, ...)`, so a zero aberration is a real no-op and a missing one is skipped. That also makes the function safe against the `None` coefficients that #342 introduces for an unmeasurable aberration — `abs(None)` would have raised `TypeError` mid-render.

**Astigmatism was rank-deficient.** `gaussian_filter1d(..., axis=0)` blurred one meridian and left the orthogonal axis sharp. Astigmatism's signature is that the tangential and sagittal foci *differ*, so both are now blurred, by different amounts, each side of the mean.

## Two of my own test premises were wrong

I corrected the tests rather than the code:

- Image-wide `std` does not scale simply with sigma — the **peak height** is the meaningful measure (∝ 1/σ²).
- `_apply_diffraction`'s sigma at 0.01 mm pitch is 0.049 px, *below* its own `max(0.1, sigma)` floor — so that comparison needs a smaller pitch to mean anything at all.

## Tests

14 tests, **13 fail without the change**: blur ordering and peak scaling across three pitches, zero and negative pitch, both key aliases, missing keys, `None` coefficients, zero as a no-op, astigmatism blurring both meridians by different amounts, and the diffraction path still scaling.

title: `get_refractive_index` raises on unvalidated Sellmeier data
body:
**File:** `src/material_database.py:336-344`

Coefficients come straight from `materials.json`, `import_csv_catalog` or `import_agf_catalog` with
no validation. Verified: `C1 = 0.25`, query 500 nm → `ZeroDivisionError`; `B1 = -5.0, C1 = 0.5`,
query 1000 nm → `ValueError: math domain error`. Neither is caught; the exception propagates through
`lens.py:311/365/384/403/411` into ray tracing and the GUI.

**Fix:** guard the denominator (`if abs(lambda_sq - mat.C1) < 1e-12: continue`), guard the sqrt, and
validate coefficients in `add_material`.

nodes.title: fix(materials): guard the Sellmeier singularities
nodes.body:
Closes #337

## Problem

Sellmeier coefficients arrive from `materials.json`, `import_csv_catalog` or `import_agf_catalog` with **no validation**, and `get_refractive_index` had two unguarded failure modes:

```
lambda_sq == C   ->  ZeroDivisionError
n_sq < 0         ->  ValueError: math domain error (in sqrt)
```

Both reproduced — `C1 = 0.25` at 500 nm, and `B1 = -5.0, C1 = 0.5` at 1000 nm. Neither was caught, so a bad catalog entry raised through `lens.py` into ray tracing and the GUI.

## Fix

A term whose denominator is within `1e-12` of zero is omitted with a warning; a non-positive `n^2` falls back to `n = 1.0` with a warning. A bad entry now degrades to a less accurate index instead of taking down the caller.

## One correction worth flagging

My first attempt *also* skipped negative Sellmeier terms. That was wrong, and the tests caught it: the third term is **legitimately negative** for real glasses, since its UV resonance sits far above the visible (`C3 = 103.56 µm²` against `lambda² = 0.35` at the d-line). Dropping it put BK7 at `n = 1.5223` instead of `1.5168` — a ~0.005 error on every lens.

Terms are now summed with signs intact. A sweep comparing old vs new across every default material × 6 wavelengths × 2 temperatures (**84 values**) is bit-identical.

## Tests

11 tests, **5 fail without the change**. The rest pin real catalog behaviour: d-line indices, normal dispersion for every real glass, the temperature correction, and explicitly that the negative UV term is still subtracted. One test drives a bad-coefficient material through `Lens.update_refractive_index`, covering the reported blast radius.

title: `load_all` calls `json.loads` on the metadata column with no error handling
body:
**File:** `src/database.py:493-496, 514-517, 591-592`

```python
if lens["metadata"]:
    meta = json.loads(lens["metadata"])
    lens.update(meta)
```

A truncated or hand-edited blob raises `JSONDecodeError` out of `load_all`.
`LensStorage.load_lenses` catches broad `Exception` (`src/gui/storage.py:99-101`) and returns `[]`, so
the user sees an **empty library** with only a log line. `lens.update(meta)` additionally raises
`TypeError`/`ValueError` if the blob is valid JSON but not an object.

**Fix:** wrap each parse in `try/except (ValueError, TypeError)` + `logger.warning`, mirroring the
existing `_coating_parse` (`:19-29`) which already does this correctly.

nodes.title: fix(db): tolerate a corrupt metadata blob instead of emptying the library
nodes.body:
Closes #338

## Problem

`load_all` called `json.loads(...[metadata])` unguarded in **three** places — a lens row, an assembly row, and a lens embedded in an assembly:

```python
if lens[metadata]:
    meta = json.loads(lens[metadata])
    lens.update(meta)
```

A truncated or hand-edited blob raised `JSONDecodeError` out of `load_all`, and `LensStorage.load_lenses` catches broad `Exception` and returns `[]` — so **one bad row left the user looking at a completely empty library**, with only a log line to explain it. Valid JSON that is not an object additionally raised from `dict.update`.

## Fix

`_metadata_merge` handles all of it, mirroring the `_coating_parse` pattern that already existed in the same file: parse inside `try/except (ValueError, TypeError)`, require an object, warn with the offending row's name, and carry on. The row keeps its real columns — only the blob is dropped.

## Verified

```
Ignoring unparseable lens bad1 metadata: Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes
load_lenses -> 2 ['Good One', 'Corrupt']        (previously: 0)
```

## Tests

11 tests. Seven cover the helper directly (valid object, truncated blob, JSON array, JSON scalar, non-string input, empty, already-parsed dict). Four cover the three load paths end to end, including a corrupt blob on the lens *inside* an assembly — the site least likely to be found by inspection.

title: Schema validators accept NaN/Inf and are dead code on the only import path
body:
**File:** `src/validation.py:869-887`; consumed at `src/gui/dialogs/startup.py:355-368`

`required_fields` checks only `isinstance`. Python's `json.load` accepts the `NaN` / `Infinity`
literals. Verified:
```
validate_lens_data_schema ACCEPTED NaN radius   ->  Lens.from_dict -> nan fl= nan
validate_lens_data_schema accepted inf thickness
```

The NaN propagates into focal length, ray tracing and the DB. `_validate_number` (`:38-65`) already
does the right finiteness check; it just isn't used here.

Separately, `validate_lens_data_schema`, `validate_lenses_json_schema`, `validate_json_file_path` and
`safe_float_conversion` have **zero call sites in `src/`** — only `tests/`. The only JSON import in
the application (`startup.py:355-374`) calls `json.load` → `Lens.from_dict` with no validation.

**Fix:** route each numeric field through `_validate_number`; call `validate_json_file_path` + the
schema validator from `startup._on_import` and `OpticalSystem.load`.

nodes.title: fix(validation): reject NaN and Infinity from parsed JSON
nodes.body:
Closes #339

## Problem

Python's `json.load` accepts the bare `NaN`, `Infinity` and `-Infinity` literals — they are not valid JSON, but they parse. `validate_lens_data_schema` checked only `isinstance`, so they sailed through:

```
BEFORE: schema ACCEPTED a NaN radius
BEFORE: focal length = nan
BEFORE: NaN == 0.0 -> False    NaN < 1.0 -> False
```

That last line is why it matters. A NaN compares false against **everything**, so it slips past every downstream threshold check silently — into focal length, ray tracing and the database.

## Fix

`_validate_number` already did the right finiteness test and simply wasn't used here. Numeric fields in the lens schema — required *and* optional — now apply the same rule, naming the field and the offending value.

A new `reject_non_finite_numbers()` walks **nested** structures, which no schema validator here covers: an assembly payload hides its radii several levels down, where a flat per-field check never sees them.

```
data['elements'][0]['lens']['thickness'] contains a non-finite number: inf
```

## The validators were also dead code

The report notes that these validators had **zero call sites in `src/`** — only tests — and that the application's one JSON import went straight from `json.load` to `Lens.from_dict`. `startup._on_import` now validates the file path, sweeps the payload for non-finite numbers, and runs the lens schema before constructing anything.

## Tests

25 tests. The module cannot import without `reject_non_finite_numbers`, so the before-state is the demonstration above rather than per-test failures. One test asserts that the NaN **really does** reach a NaN focal length — so the premise can't quietly lapse — and another asserts `json.loads('{"x": NaN}')` really does produce a NaN. The rest cover every required and optional numeric field, nested payloads, booleans not being read as numbers (bool is an int subclass), and that the existing type/missing-field errors are unchanged.

title: `safe_float_conversion` raises `OverflowError` instead of returning `(False, default)`
body:
**File:** `src/validation.py:536-540`

```python
result = float(value)          # float(10**400) raises OverflowError
```

**Repro (verified):** `safe_float_conversion(10**400)` → `OverflowError: int too large to convert to
float`. A JSON integer literal reaches this path. The string branch (`:543-549`) only catches
`ValueError`, so the same gap exists there. The function's contract is "never raises".

**Fix:** `except (ValueError, OverflowError): return False, default`.

nodes.title: fix(validation): honour safe_float_conversion's never-raises contract
nodes.body:
Closes #340

## Problem

`safe_float_conversion`'s contract is that it **never raises** — every caller consumes the `(success, value)` tuple. But the int/float branch called `float(value)` unguarded, and `float()` on a large int raises rather than returning `inf`:

```python
safe_float_conversion(10**400)   # OverflowError: int too large to convert to float
```

A JSON integer literal reaches this path. The string branch only caught `ValueError`, so the same gap existed there.

## Fix

Both branches catch `(ValueError, OverflowError, TypeError)`. The NaN/inf rejection and the bool rejection are untouched, so valid values still convert and a custom `default` is still honoured.

## Tests

Five tests added to `tests/test_validation.py`, **four fail without the change**: the two huge-int cases and the two subtests inside a never-raises sweep over 15 inputs (`None`, containers, `object()`, `'1e999'`, infinities, NaN…). Two further tests pin that valid values still convert and that boundary floats are still rejected — the guard must not over-reject.

title: A single bad entry in `materials.json` discards every material after it
body:
**File:** `src/material_database.py:281-287`

```python
try:
    with open(self.db_path, "r") as f:
        data = json.load(f)
        for name, mat_data in data.items():
            self.materials[name] = MaterialProperties.from_dict(mat_data)
except Exception as e:
    logger.warning("Could not load material database: %s", e)
```

`from_dict` is `cls(**data)` (`:74-76`) with no key/type validation, so one unknown key raises
`TypeError` and the loop aborts mid-file. The user gets a warning plus a silently truncated material
list. `open()` also has no `encoding=`.

**Fix:** validate each entry in its own `try/except`, warn per entry and continue.

nodes.title: fix(materials): load each catalog entry independently
nodes.body:
Closes #341

## Problem

`_load_database` looped over the JSON inside a **single** `try/except`, and `MaterialProperties.from_dict` is `cls(**data)` with no key filtering:

```python
try:
    with open(self.db_path, "r") as f:
        data = json.load(f)
        for name, mat_data in data.items():
            self.materials[name] = MaterialProperties.from_dict(mat_data)
except Exception as e:
    logger.warning("Could not load material database: %s", e)
```

One unknown key raises `TypeError`, aborts the loop mid-file, and leaves a warning plus a silently truncated material list. Since the built-in defaults are loaded first, **nothing visibly looks wrong** — the catalog just appears short.

## Worse than reported

Reproduced with entries missing a required field (`catalog`): the **first** entry raised, so *every* entry in the file was discarded:

```
Could not load material database: MaterialProperties.__init__() missing 1 required positional argument: 'catalog'
materials loaded: ['BK7', 'E-FD60', 'F2', 'FUSEDSILICA', 'N-BK7', 'S-LAH79', 'SF11']   <- defaults only
silently lost:   ['AAA', 'BBB', 'CCC', 'DDD']                                          <- the entire file
```

## Fix

Each entry is validated in its own `try/except`, logging the offending name and reason, with a skipped-entry count reported at the end. Also:

- non-object entries are skipped with a clear message instead of raising deep inside the constructor
- valid JSON that is not an object is ignored rather than iterated
- the file is opened as UTF-8, so a non-ASCII name does not raise `UnicodeDecodeError`

```
Loaded 10 material(s) from /tmp/...json; skipped 2 unusable entries
loaded from file: ['AAA', 'BBB', 'CCC']      (BAD + NOTADICT skipped)
```

## Tests

9 tests in `tests/test_material_database_resilience.py`; 3 fail without the change — the reported worst case (a lone bad entry), a bad entry in the middle of a good catalog, and a non-object entry.

title: Broad `except Exception` handlers convert trace failures into "perfect optics"
body:
**File:** `src/aberrations.py:283-285, 325-327, 709-711, 802-804`

```python
except Exception as e:
    logger.warning("Field estimators ray trace failed: %s", e)
    return 0.0, 0.0
```

A failure is reported as **coma = 0.0 and astigmatism = 0.0** — i.e. better than diffraction
limited — with only a `WARNING` log line. Given T-01/T-02, this is a live path: the 2D tracer
returns `MISSED` instead of raising, so these paths silently publish zeros for exactly the geometries
that are broken.

**Fix:** return `None` (or `NaN`) and have `calculate_all_aberrations` set a `valid=False` flag, so
the GUI can grey out the value.

nodes.title: fix(aberrations): report an unmeasurable metric as missing, not as zero
nodes.body:
Closes #342

## Problem

`_calculate_field_estimators` wrapped its whole body in `except Exception … return 0.0, 0.0`, so a failed ray trace reported:

```
coma = 0.0, astigmatism = 0.0
```

That is **indistinguishable from a perfect off-axis design** — and *better* than diffraction limited — for exactly the geometries whose trace failed. It is a live path: the 2D tracer returns `MISSED` instead of raising, so these lines were reached in practice.

```
before:  failed trace  -> coma=0.0      astig=0.0     <- fictional perfection
after:   failed trace  -> valid=False coma=None astig=None
```

## Fix

The estimators return `None`. **On-axis stays a genuine `(0.0, 0.0)`** — there is no coma at zero field, which is a measurement, not a gap.

`calculate_all_aberrations` derives a `valid` flag from every metric. The report formats each metric with `:.4f`, which a `None` would crash, so a `_fmt` helper renders missing values as `N/A` and the report gains a WARNING block driven by the calculator's own verdict.

## Three follow-on corrections found while testing

- The system path substituted a **block of `0.0`** when `field_data` was `None`, so a failed *system* trace still looked perfect. It now keeps `None`.
- My first `_all_valid` compared the dict against `None` instead of its values, so the system `valid` flag could never go `False`. Caught by a test asserting a dict containing a `None` is invalid.
- The zero-power branch publishes placeholders rather than measurements, so it now sets `valid: False` explicitly.

## Scope

The other three broad-`except` sites named in the issue — `calculate_field_metrics`, `calculate_spot_rms`, `_calculate_spherical_aberration` — **already returned `None`** and are untouched.

## Tests

22 tests covering the helper, the estimators, the singlet and system paths, the zero-power branch, and the report formatting.

title: Edge thickness is evaluated at the mechanical diameter, not the clear aperture
body:
**File:** `src/lens.py:535-567`

```python
def calculate_edge_thickness(self) -> Optional[float]:
    """Calculate the rim (edge) thickness at the clear aperture. ..."""
    h = self.diameter / 2
```

The docstring's first sentence contradicts its own third. A lens with
`clear_aperture_1/2 < diameter` gets its manufacturability judged at a radius the lens is never
polished to — and `MIN_EDGE_THICKNESS` validation in `validation.py` inherits this.
`LensGeometry._minimum_thickness` (`geometry.py:226`) has the same assumption.

**Fix:** `h = min(self.get_clear_aperture_1(), self.get_clear_aperture_2()) / 2`, or reword the
docstring.

nodes.title: fix(lens): judge edge thickness at the radius the lens is polished to
nodes.body:
Closes #343

## Problem

`calculate_edge_thickness` documented itself as evaluating *"at the clear aperture"* while using `h = self.diameter / 2` — the **mechanical** radius. Its own first sentence contradicted its third.

A lens is never polished out to its blank, so judging material at `diameter / 2` assesses a height the finished part does not reach.

## The failure mode is a false rejection

For `R1=40, R2=-40, t=2.0, D=30` with an 8 mm clear aperture:

```
at the mechanical h=15 : edge = -3.8380  -> "surfaces intersect", REJECTED
at the real clear h=4  : edge = +1.5990  -> perfectly manufacturable
```

A good lens, refused.

## Fix

New `Lens.get_manufacturing_radius()` — the smaller of the two clear apertures and the mechanical radius, ignoring unset, non-finite and non-positive values. A lens without a clear aperture behaves **exactly** as before.

`MIN_EDGE_THICKNESS` validation inherited the bug through its probe `Lens`, so **`check_physical_feasibility` owns that probe** (not `validate_lens_parameters`) and gained optional `clear_aperture_1`/`clear_aperture_2` parameters. `validate_lens_parameters` gained the same keywords so a caller can supply them. `LensGeometry._minimum_thickness` had the same assumption in its radius set.

## A mistake worth recording

My first attempt put the probe kwargs in `validate_lens_parameters`, which has **no probe**. The undefined names raised `NameError` inside `check_physical_feasibility`'s `except Exception`, which swallowed it into *"geometry is undefined"* — and broke **seven pre-existing feasibility tests**. Caught by running the existing suite rather than only my new tests. The parameters now live on the function that owns the probe.

## Tests

17 tests, **10 fail without the change**. One pins that the chosen test case really does evaluate *negative* at the blank radius, so the regression can't quietly lapse into asserting nothing. Others cover the no-clear-aperture path being byte-identical, the clamp when the clear aperture exceeds the blank, one-sided apertures, `None` still returned for an overhanging aperture, and `default Lens()` remaining feasible.

title: 2D parabolic normal and 2D parabolic intersection use different apertures
body:
**File:** `src/tracer_2d.py:113-119 & 127-132` vs `:213`

```python
# normal
r_max = self.D / 2                     # mechanical D
a = self.parabolic_sag_1 / (r_max * r_max)
# intersection
r_max = self.D / 2 if semi_aperture is None else semi_aperture   # CA1/2
a = sag / (r_max * r_max)
```

`_intersect_front_surface` passes `semi = self.CA1 / 2` (`:324, 330-332`), so the *intersection point*
is computed on one parabola while the *surface normal* is computed from another. Any lens with
`is_parabolic_1/2 = True` **and** `clear_aperture_N != diameter` is refracted with a normal from a
different conic than the one it hit. The 3D tracer does not have this bug (`tracer_3d.py:393, 439`).

**Fix:** use `self.get_effective_radius_1() / _2()` (the vertex radius) in both places.

nodes.title: fix(tracer2d): intersect the parabolic surface on the conic the normal uses
nodes.body:
Closes #344

## Problem

`parabolic_sag_N` is documented as the sag at the **mechanical** radius `D/2`, and both `Lens.get_effective_radius_N` and `_surface_normal_angle` use that radius. The intersection built its conic from the *clear aperture* instead:

```
normal:        a = sag / (D/2)^2
intersection:  a = sag / (CA/2)^2
```

`_intersect_front_surface` passes `semi = CA1/2`, so any lens with `is_parabolic_N` **and** `clear_aperture_N != diameter` was refracted with a normal from a different conic than the one it hit.

Verified — a ray aimed at `y = 3.0` on the defining conic:

```
before:  lands at y = 3.0973   <- not on the conic
after:   lands at y = 3.0000
```

## I did not use the fix the issue suggests

It proposes `get_effective_radius_N() / 2` in both places. That **does not reconcile them either**:

```
issue suggestion:  a = 0.005243
the normal uses:   a = 0.012800
```

`get_effective_radius` returns the vertex *radius of curvature*, not the radius the sag was quoted at. A test pins that arithmetic so the suggestion isn't silently retried later.

## What I did instead

The intersection uses `D/2` for the conic and treats `semi_aperture` purely as a **vignetting limit** — which is exactly how `_intersect_sphere_surface` already treats its own `semi_aperture`. So the geometry is defined once and the clear aperture still does its actual job:

```
ray aimed at y=6 on a lens with a 10mm clear aperture -> still MISS (beyond the 5.0 limit)
ray aimed at y=4.5                                    -> passes
```

## Tests

11 tests, **3 fail without the change**: the hit lies on the normal's conic at y = 1, 2 and 3; the conic `a` matches; the clear aperture still vignettes and tracks its value; and the flat-sag fallback and spherical path are untouched.

title: Optimum checks in `optimize_simulated_annealing` and `optimize_genetic` are unguarded
body:
**File:** `src/global_optimizer.py:71, 142, 254`

```python
71:  scale_factor = max(0.01, min(1.0, temperature / initial_temperature))
142: iterations=iteration + 1 + local_result.iterations
254: selected_indices = random.sample(range(len(population)), k)   # k=3 default
```

Verified: `initial_temperature <= 0` → `ZeroDivisionError`; `max_iterations <= 0` →
`UnboundLocalError: iteration`; `population_size < 3` → `ValueError: Sample larger than population`
(the GUI is one config change away from the last one).

**Fix:** clamp `initial_temperature > 0`; initialise `iteration = -1`; clamp `k = min(k, len(population))`.

nodes.title: fix(optimizer): guard degenerate global-optimizer configurations
nodes.body:
Closes #345

## Problem — three degenerate configurations, all reproduced

```
initial_temperature = 0  ->  ZeroDivisionError: float division by zero
max_iterations = 0       ->  UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable
                              'iteration' where it is not associated with a value
population_size < 3      ->  ValueError: Sample larger than population
```

The third needs **no bad input at all**: `k=3` is the default tournament size, so `population_size=2` — a perfectly ordinary configuration, one GUI spin-box change away — raised. All three were one config change away.

## Fix

- **`initial_temperature <= 0`** is clamped to a small positive value with a warning rather than rejected. `temperature / initial_temperature` is evaluated *every* iteration, and a near-zero starting temperature is a reasonable thing for a caller to mean.
- **`iteration` is seeded to `-1`** so the post-loop iteration count reads 0 instead of raising when `max_iterations <= 0` leaves the loop body unentered.
- **`_tournament_select` clamps `k`** to the population size, and raises a clear `ValueError` on an empty population rather than `random.sample`'s message.

## Verified

All four degenerate configurations now run, and the search still reaches the same optimum:

```
initial_temperature=0 -> ok, iterations=21
max_iterations=0      -> ok, iterations=20
population_size=2     -> ok, merit 0.9234 -> 0.8392
population_size=1     -> ok, merit 0.8392
```

## Tests

16 tests, **10 fail without the change**. They cover zero/negative/tiny temperature, zero/negative iterations, populations of 1 and 2, the `k` clamp against an empty population, and that the guard does not degrade search quality — a 2-member population must still improve the merit.

One of my own assertions was wrong and I corrected the test rather than the code: with `max_iterations=0` I expected the final merit to equal the initial one, but the *local simplex refinement* still runs and improves it. That's correct behaviour, so the test now asserts the result is well-formed instead.

title: Simplex convergence is scale-blind; zero variables reports false success
body:
**File:** `src/optimizer.py:420, 456-457, 509-521`

```python
merit_range = merit_values[-1] - merit_values[0]
if merit_range < tolerance:      # tolerance=1e-6 ABSOLUTE
```

With geometry penalties at `1e8` (`:239, 251, 255, 265, 284, 290`) a `1e-6` absolute spread is far
below floating-point resolution at that magnitude, so the run always burns the full `max_iterations`
while claiming convergence semantics. Symmetrically, with `len(self.variables) == 0` the simplex has
one vertex, `merit_range == 0`, and the loop breaks immediately.

**Repro (verified):** `GlobalOptimizer(sys, [], [target]).optimize()` returns `success=True`,
`"Converged after 1 iterations"` without evaluating or changing anything.

**Fix:** use a relative criterion; reject an empty variable list up front with `ValueError`.

nodes.title: fix(optimizer): make the simplex convergence test scale-blind
nodes.body:
Closes #346

## Two defects

**1. The convergence test was absolute.**

```python
merit_range = merit_values[-1] - merit_values[0]
if merit_range < tolerance:      # tolerance=1e-6 ABSOLUTE
```

Geometry penalties reach `1e8`, where the spacing between adjacent floats is already **~4e-8**. An absolute `1e-6` spread therefore sits below the representation floor and cannot fire while the merit is large.

**2. An empty variable list "converged" instantly.**

With `len(self.variables) == 0` the simplex has one vertex, `merit_range` is identically 0, and the loop broke on iteration 1 having evaluated and changed nothing:

```
GlobalOptimizer(sys, [], [target]).optimize()
-> success=True, "Converged after 1 iterations"
```

## Fix

The threshold now scales with the merit's own magnitude:

```
merit_range <= max(tolerance * max|merit|, MIN_MERIT_RANGE)
```

At merit `1e8` a spread of 100 counts as convergence; at merit ~1 the threshold is `1e-6` exactly as before, so ordinary runs are untouched. The `MIN_MERIT_RANGE` floor keeps the test usable when the merit is near zero and the product underflows.

An empty variable list now raises `ValueError` up front.

## Honest scoping of claim 1

The measurable effect is **wasted work**, not a wrong answer:

```
before: 21 iterations
after:   7 iterations      (same optimum, same message)
```

I could not construct a case where the reported *outcome* changes. In the scenario I could build, the out-of-bounds abort path fires before the convergence break, and a run that escapes the penalty region drops to order-1 merits where the absolute test worked anyway. Claim 2 is unambiguous and independently valuable.

## Tests

14 tests, **10 fail without the change**: the scale-blind threshold at 1e8 (accepting a spread of 50, rejecting 5e5), unchanged semantics for order-1 merits, the zero-merit floor, negative merits, the 3× iteration reduction, all four empty-variable-list paths, and that a single variable still works fine.

title: Unbounded merit cache plus a full `deepcopy` of the system per cache miss
body:
**File:** `src/optimizer.py:646-654, 659`

```python
cache_key = tuple(round(v, 10) for v in values)
self._merit_cache[cache_key] = merit
system = copy.deepcopy(self.system)
```

Every simplex vertex is a distinct point, so the hit rate is ~0 and the cache grows without bound for
the process lifetime while contributing nothing. Measured: 25 simplex iterations → 37 cache entries,
1.48 s, essentially all of it in `deepcopy` + the aberration/spot trace.

**Fix:** drop the cache (or bound it with an LRU), and mutate a single reusable system in place
instead of deep-copying per evaluation — `_apply_variables` is the only thing that needs the copy
(for the *returned* result), not the merit evaluation.

nodes.title: fix(optimizer): bound the merit cache
nodes.body:
Closes #347

## Problem

`_evaluate_design` cached every design it saw in a plain dict that lived for the process lifetime:

```python
cache_key = tuple(round(v, 10) for v in values)
if cache_key in self._merit_cache:
    merit = self._merit_cache[cache_key]
else:
    ...
    self._merit_cache[cache_key] = merit
```

Every simplex vertex is a distinct point, so the hit rate there is only ~12% — 25 simplex iterations left **59 entries**, growing forever.

## I bounded it rather than dropping it

The issue offers "drop the cache (or bound it with an LRU)". Dropping it would cost real evaluations, because the hit rate is **not** zero:

```
simplex            12%
gradient descent   33%
```

Gradient descent re-evaluates the same point when it backtracks to a smaller step, and simplex shrink re-evaluates the best vertex.

So: capped at `MERIT_CACHE_MAX` (4096) with **FIFO** eviction — dicts preserve insertion order, so the oldest key is first, and a precise LRU would cost more bookkeeping than it saves at this hit rate.

The lookup also became a single `.get`, which must be `is not None` rather than truthy — a merit of `0.0` is a real merit. A test pins that.

## I declined the other suggestion, because the measurement doesn't support it

The issue attributes most of the evaluation cost to `deepcopy`. Measured over 25 evaluations:

```
25 evaluations      : 0.954 s
25 deepcopies alone : 0.003 s   (0.3%)
```

The cost is the **aberration and spot trace**, not the copy. Reusing a single system would save ~0.3% while introducing aliasing between the scratch system and `merit_function`'s own reference. A test asserts the copy stays a small fraction of evaluation time, so the claim stays honest if that ratio ever changes.

## Tests

12 tests, **4 fail without the change**: the cap holds under 200 distinct evaluations and under a full simplex run, the cap is the documented class default, FIFO evicts the oldest key, and recent entries survive. Others confirm hits still work, a cached value equals a fresh computation, and similar-but-distinct designs are not confused.

title: `globals()` indirection + `except: pass` turn real bugs into `INFEASIBLE_MERIT`
body:
**File:** `src/optimizer.py:164-172, 174-199`

```python
try:
    if "SpotDiagram" in globals():
        spot = globals()["SpotDiagram"](system)
...
except Exception:
    pass
return INFEASIBLE_MERIT
```

The `globals()` dance makes the dependency invisible to linters and readers, and the bare `pass`
discards the exception entirely — a `KeyError` from a malformed spot result and a genuine geometry
failure produce the identical, indistinguishable `1e9`.

**Fix:** import the names directly at module scope; `except Exception as e: logger.warning("...%s", e)`.

nodes.title: fix(optimizer): name the merit dependencies instead of globals()-ing them
nodes.body:
Closes #348

## Problem

Both evaluator helpers looked their dependencies up in `globals()`:

```python
if "SpotDiagram" in globals():
    spot = globals()["SpotDiagram"](system)
...
except Exception:
    pass
```

**The names are already imported at module scope** — `SpotDiagram` from `.analysis`, `PSFCalculator`/`WavefrontSensor`/`NUMPY_AVAILABLE` from `.analysis.beam_synthesis`. So every `"X" in globals()` test was dead weight that hid the dependency from readers *and* from linters. In `_eval_mtf` it was spelled:

```python
"PSFCalculator" in globals() and "WavefrontSensor" in globals()
and "NUMPY_AVAILABLE" in globals() and globals()["NUMPY_AVAILABLE"]
```

whose first three halves are always true and whose last was a verbose way of writing `if not NUMPY_AVAILABLE`.

**And the bare `except Exception: pass` discarded the exception entirely.** A `KeyError` from a malformed spot result and a genuine geometry failure both collapsed to the same `INFEASIBLE_MERIT` with no trace — you could not tell a broken evaluator from a legitimately infeasible design.

## Fix

Names used directly; every caught exception logged. The level split is deliberate:

```
malformed / vignetted spot -> DEBUG    "no usable spot (rms_radius=..., valid_rays=...)"
raised exception           -> WARNING  "RMS spot merit evaluation failed: <reason>"
```

A vignetted or short spot result is a **routine** outcome during a run — it fires many times per optimization — so warning on it would bury the log. An unexpected exception is not, and warning is what makes it findable.

## Tests

12 tests, **6 fail without the change**. The central one asserts the two failure modes produce the *same merit but different log messages* — which is the entire point of the fix. Others assert no runtime `globals()` remains (comments stripped, so the explanatory note doesn't trip it), that the dependencies are module-level names, and that the `NUMPY_AVAILABLE` guard is genuinely consulted.

title: `optimize_gradient_descent` accepts every step and has no bounds or line search
body:
**File:** `src/optimizer.py:553-555, 569-582`

```python
553: for iteration in range(max_iterations):
554:     last_iteration = iteration
555:     last_iteration = iteration        # <- dead duplicate
...
569: improvement = initial_merit - new_merit        # shadowed at :582
574: current_values = new_values                    # accepted unconditionally
```

Every step is accepted even when the merit got worse, with no backtracking and no bound handling — on
a merit with `1e8` geometry penalties the trajectory diverges. The convergence test compares against
`merit_history[-1]`, which is not updated on the iteration that breaks.

**Fix:** reject steps that increase the merit (halve the learning rate and retry), bound-check before
applying, delete the dead lines, compare against the *current* merit.

nodes.title: fix(optimizer): gradient descent must reject steps that worsen the merit
nodes.body:
Closes #349

## Problem

`optimize_gradient_descent` accepted every step unconditionally:

```python
new_values = [val - learning_rate * grad ...]
new_merit = self._evaluate_design(new_values)
improvement = initial_merit - new_merit      # shadowed, never read
if abs(new_merit - merit_history[-1]) < tolerance:
    break
current_values = new_values                  # accepted regardless
```

No backtracking, no bound handling. On a merit carrying large geometry penalties the trajectory **diverges**.

## Verified

On a design starting at 0.2 mm thickness, whose merit is dominated by a geometry penalty (~2e8):

```
before: merit 2.00e+08 -> 3.06e+30, improvement -1.5e+27 %
after:  merit 2.00e+08 -> 2.00e+08, improvement      0.00 %
```

Twenty-two orders of magnitude, and a reported "improvement" of −1.5×10²⁷ %.

## Fix

A step that does not reduce the merit is rejected: halve the step size, retry from the same point, up to `MAX_BACKTRACKING_STEPS` (12), giving up below `MIN_LEARNING_RATE`. If no smaller step helps, that is a stationary point — or a numerical gradient already below the tolerance — and the run stops rather than wandering into a worse design.

Bounds stay **penalties, not walls** (variables are not clamped), so an out-of-range trial simply scores badly and is rejected by the same test. `result.success` still reports final validity.

## Three further corrections

- **`merit_history[-1]` was the wrong reference.** The history is only appended for *accepted* steps, so on a stalled run its last entry can predate the design actually returned — both for the convergence comparison and for `final_merit`. `current_merit` is now tracked explicitly.
- `last_iteration = iteration` appeared **twice** in the loop body.
- `improvement = initial_merit - new_merit` was computed then overwritten at the end of the method without ever being read.

## Tests

16 tests, **8 fail without the change**: monotone merit history, convergence at lr = 5.0 and lr = 500.0, no divergence from a penalised start, `improvement` never absurdly negative, `final_merit` matching the returned design (including on a stalled run), history and variable history staying in step, and reflection tests pinning the three dead-code removals.

title: `optimize_gradient_descent` / SA write state into caller-owned dataclasses
body:
**File:** `src/global_optimizer.py:123, 231`

```python
self._apply_variables(best_values)        # return value dropped — pure no-op
for i, val in enumerate(best_values):
    self.variables[i].current_value = val  # <- this is what actually works
```

`_apply_variables` (`optimizer.py:656-673`) returns a deepcopy and never mutates `self.system`, so
lines 123/231 are dead code. The state transfer happens **only** through mutation of the caller's
`OptimizationVariable` objects — which `gui/tabs/optimization_tab.py:125` then also reads and
applies, so the GUI's saved variable values silently become the SA/GA result rather than the user's
inputs.

**Fix:** delete the dead calls; pass `best_values` explicitly into `optimize_simplex(start=best_values)`;
`copy.deepcopy(self.variables)` before mutating.

nodes.title: fix(optimizer): pass the refinement start explicitly instead of mutating caller state
nodes.body:
Closes #350

## Problem

Both global optimizers finished their search with:

```python
self._apply_variables(best_values)          # return value dropped
for i, val in enumerate(best_values):
    self.variables[i].current_value = val    # this is what actually worked
local_result = self.optimize_simplex(max_iterations=50)
```

`_apply_variables` returns a **deepcopy** and never mutates `self.system`, so those calls were **dead code**.

The state transfer happened *only* through mutation of the **caller's** `OptimizationVariable` objects — which `optimization_tab.py` also reads and saves. So running simulated annealing or the genetic algorithm silently replaced the user's inputs with the search result.

## Verified

```
simulated annealing caller vars [50.0] -> [52.01002132572631]  mutated
genetic             caller vars [50.0] -> [59.466763858241826]  mutated
```

After, with **identical** optimization results (merit 0.8392 either way — the search itself was never the problem):

```
simulated annealing caller vars [50.0] -> [50.0]  not mutated
genetic             caller vars [50.0] -> [50.0]  not mutated
```

## Fix

`optimize_simplex` gained an explicit `start` parameter — validated against the variable count, and **copied rather than aliased** so a later caller-side edit cannot corrupt a running simplex. Both call sites use it; the two dead `_apply_variables` calls are gone.

## Tests

12 tests, **7 fail without the change**. One pins the *premise* of the dead-code claim — that `_apply_variables` really is a pure function of its argument — so those two calls cannot be reintroduced as if they worked. Others assert the caller's variables and every other variable attribute survive untouched, that optimization still improves the merit, and reflection tests confirm no `_apply_variables` call or `current_value = val` assignment remains in `global_optimizer.py`.

title: Beam synthesis: off-by-one beamlet spacing and `q` propagated with the wrong λ in glass
body:
**File:** `src/analysis/beam_synthesis.py:340, 357-358, 62-63, 445-448`

```python
340: delta = ep_diam / grid_size
357: y_vals = np.linspace(-max_r, max_r, grid_size)
```

Actual spacing is `2*max_r/(grid_size-1) = ep_diam/(grid_size-1)` — a 3 % error at `grid_size=32`
that directly sets the beamlet waist `w0 = 1.5*delta` (`:342`).

```python
 62: self.q_x += distance        # GaussianBeam.propagate — always free-space lambda, full d
447: beam.q_x += dist            # inside the glass: needs d/n
```

`q` is defined with the *local* wavelength, so on entering `n=1.5168` the reduced `q'` should be
scaled by `n1/n2` and the propagation length by `1/n`. Verified: `w_x` 0.1323 → 0.1621 mm across an
`n=1.0→1.5, R=50` surface.

Also `class np: ndarray = Any` (`:13-14`) has no `array()`, so the "graceful degradation" returns at
`:129`, `:285`, `:334` raise `AttributeError: type object 'np' has no attribute 'array'` when numpy
is missing — the exact opposite of graceful. `NUMPY_AVAILABLE` is checked at `:284`/`:329` but not `:129`.

**Fix:** use `dx = 2*max_r/(grid_size-1)`; track the local wavelength/index on `GaussianBeam` and
use `q' = n1/n2 * q` with `d/n` propagation; define a real fallback or raise a clean `ImportError`.

nodes.title: fix(beam): correct beamlet spacing, track the local medium, degrade honestly
nodes.body:
Closes #351

## Three defects

**1. Beamlet spacing was 3.1% wrong.**

```python
delta = ep_diam / grid_size
```

The grid is `np.linspace(-max_r, max_r, grid_size)`, which spans `2*max_r` in **`grid_size - 1`** intervals:

```
grid=8    -12.50%
grid=32    -3.125%     <- the issue's figure
grid=64    -1.562%
```

That error went straight into the waist `w0 = 1.5 * delta`.

**2. `q` is defined against the local medium — and two things weren't.**

`refract()` already used the reduced form `1/q' = (n1/n2)(1/q) - Phi/n2`, but:

- `propagate` advanced `q` by `d`, not `d/n` — a beam crossing a thick element propagated as if in air.
- `GaussianBeam` carried the **vacuum** wavelength forever, while `w = sqrt(-λ_local / (π·Im(1/q)))` with `λ_local = λ_vac/n`. So every beam radius after entering glass was too large by `n`:

```
before:  w_x 0.1323 -> 0.1621 mm across an n=1.0->1.5, R=50 surface
after:   w_x 0.100000 -> 0.100000  (continuous)
```

`GaussianBeam` now tracks `n` and updates `wavelength` on refraction. The new `advance_q()` does the index-aware advance **without moving the ray** — the BSP tracer has already moved it, so `propagate()` would double-count. The BSP propagator also passes `beam.n` as `n1` instead of a hardcoded `1.0`, which was wrong for every element after the first in an assembly.

**3. Graceful degradation wasn't.**

The numpy stand-in declared only `ndarray`, so every "return an empty result" path raised:

```
AttributeError: type object 'np' has no attribute 'array'
```

It now provides `array`/`zeros`/`ones`/`linspace`/`meshgrid` returning plain lists — all an empty-result caller can use. The genuinely numpy-requiring BSP path still raises its clean `ImportError`, and a test asserts it does.

## Tests

21 tests, **13 fail without the change**: `w_x` continuity across curved *and* flat surfaces, vacuum-wavelength preservation over one and two surfaces and a round trip, `d/n` propagation in glass vs `d` in air, both axes advancing, `advance_q` not moving the ray, and three subprocess tests with numpy genuinely blocked.

title: Diffraction PSF/MTF frequency scale is off by `N/(N-1)`
body:
**File:** `src/analysis/psf_mtf.py:269-273` and `:458-462`

```python
grid_size = wf.W.shape[0]              # N
dx_pupil = L_grid / grid_size
```

`WavefrontSensor` builds the grid with `np.linspace(-max_r, max_r, grid_size)`
(`diffraction_psf.py:72-73`), whose spacing is `ep_diam/(grid_size-1)`.

**Repro (verified):** the code reports `df = 14.4317 lp/mm`; the correct value is
`25/63/(550e-6*49.213) = 14.6610 lp/mm` — a 1.6 % error at `grid_size=64`. The same 1.6 % inflates
`raw_extent` in `_calculate_diffraction_psf`, shifting the resample window.

**Fix:** `dx_pupil = 2*max_r/(grid_size - 1)` in both places, or have `get_pupil_wavefront` return
the spacing.

nodes.title: fix(psf): use the pupil sample spacing, not the sample count
nodes.body:
Closes #352

## Problem

The pupil grid is built as `np.linspace(-max_r, max_r, N)` — **N samples spanning `2*max_r` across `N-1` intervals**. Both frequency sites divided the pupil width by `N` instead of `N-1`:

```python
# psf_mtf.py:269
grid_size = wf.W.shape[0]  # N
dx_pupil = L_grid / grid_size          # should be / (grid_size - 1)

# psf_mtf.py:458
dx_pupil = ep_diam / N_pupil           # should be / (N_pupil - 1)
```

Every reported spatial frequency was low by a factor of `N/(N-1)` — 1.6% at `grid_size=64`. Site 1 sets the MTF frequency axis; site 2 feeds `dx_psf` and therefore `raw_extent`, so the same error inflated the PSF extent and shifted the resample window.

```
correct  dx=0.396825 -> df=14.6608 lp/mm
current  dx=0.390625 -> df=14.4317 lp/mm
ratio N/(N-1) = 1.015873
```

## Fix

Both use `width / (N - 1)`, and both guard `N > 1` so a single-sample grid cannot divide by zero. The long comment block above site 1 (which reasoned its way to the wrong formula) now records where the spacing actually comes from.

## Verified

```
efl = 90.907434
reported df            = 7.936653
expected 25/(N-1)/(l*f) = 7.936653
old      25/N/(l*f)     = 7.812642
ratio reported/expected = 1.000000000
```

## Tests

4 tests in `tests/test_psf_mtf.py`; 3 fail without the change. One test pins the formula to the grid size the sensor actually builds, since `calculate_mtf` hardcodes `pupil_grid_size=64` and the sampling is not caller-tunable.

title: `.astype(int)` in the PSF resampler biases every sample left of centre
body:
**File:** `src/analysis/psf_mtf.py:480-481`

```python
idx_y = ((Y_target + raw_extent / 2) / dx_psf).astype(int)
idx_z = ((Z_target + raw_extent / 2) / dx_psf).astype(int)
```

`int()` rounds toward zero, so for negative coordinates every sample is biased by up to a full pixel
(half a pixel on average). `dx_psf == 0` (empty system) → division by zero.

**Fix:** `.astype(np.int64)` after `np.floor(...)`; add an `N_pupil == 0` guard.

nodes.title: fix(psf): floor the resample indices and refuse a degenerate spacing
nodes.body:
Closes #353

## I could not reproduce a visible bug here, and the tests say so

Two problems were filed:

1. `astype(int)` truncates toward zero → bias for negative coordinates
2. `dx_psf == 0` → division by zero

**Neither changes any output today.** Rather than quietly claim a fix, here is
the evidence:

**The truncation is masked by the clip.** `astype(int)` differs from `floor` *only* for negative values — and the result is clipped immediately afterwards:

```python
idx = np.clip(idx, 0, padded_N - 1)
```

so every negative index becomes `0` either way. Sweeping `-200.7 .. 200.7`:

```
raw differ at    : 201 of 401
differ after clip: 0
```

A before/after dump of the resampled image across six sensor/pixel combinations is **identical**.

**The zero division is unreachable in practice.** `dx_psf == 0` requires `wavelength_nm == 0`, which already divides by zero upstream in the wavefront — so the PSF is zeroed before the resampler runs. The old code produced an all-zero image anyway.

## What I landed anyway

- `floor` instead of truncation — the right index for a nearest-below sample, so correctness no longer *depends* on the clip staying.
- A guard for non-finite/non-positive `dx_psf` that returns an explicit, logged empty PSF instead of a silent constant-garbage image.
- Extracted `_map_to_raw_indices()` so the mapping is directly testable rather than buried in a method body.

## Deliberately not touched

`raw_extent = padded_N * dx_psf` counts **N** intervals where the grid has **N-1**. That shifts the resample window and makes the index mapping asymmetric about the centre. It is the same off-by-one already corrected in two *other* places in this file — but it is a **different defect** from the one filed, so I left it alone rather than folding it into this PR silently. Worth its own issue.

## Tests

12 tests, including two that record the *inert* findings above, so the next reader does not have to re-derive them.

title: `MonteCarloAnalyzer.run` divides by `num_trials` unguarded; `criterion` is decorative
body:
**File:** `src/tolerancing.py:429, 462-465, 485, 495`

```python
485: yield_pct = (pass_count / num_trials) * 100      # ZeroDivisionError for num_trials=0
462: results = spot.trace_spot(...)                   # no try/except in run()
495: "criterion": criterion,                          # echoed, never used
```

Verified: `run(criterion="something_else")` returns `criterion: 'something_else'` with unchanged RMS
statistics. A single TIR/exception aborts the run and all accumulated `self.results` are lost
(`_spot_rms` at `:367-372` does wrap the trace in `try/except → inf`; `run()` does not).

**Fix:** route `run()` through `self._spot_rms(...)`; guard `num_trials`; either implement
`criterion` dispatch or raise `ValueError` for anything but `rms_spot_radius`.

nodes.title: fix(tolerancing): stop run() dividing by zero and losing runs to one TIR
nodes.body:
Closes #354

## Three defects in `MonteCarloAnalyzer.run`

**1. ZeroDivisionError.** `yield_pct = (pass_count / num_trials) * 100` with `num_trials=0`. Now a `ValueError` naming the parameter.

**2. `criterion` was decorative.** It was accepted, echoed into the results dict, and never used — so `run(criterion="something_else")` returned unchanged RMS statistics *under that label*. A caller asking for an MTF yield got a spot-radius yield that appeared to agree with what they asked for. Only `rms_spot_radius` is implemented, so anything else now raises `ValueError`. The supported name lives in `SUPPORTED_CRITERIA` rather than in a default argument plus a comparison, so the two cannot drift apart.

**3. One TIR lost the entire run.** The trial loop called `spot.trace_spot()` directly while `_spot_rms` — which already wraps the trace and maps a vignetted result or any exception to `inf` — sat unused. The nominal trace had the same unguarded shape. Both now route through `_spot_rms`, so a failing trial is scored as the failure it is and surviving trials are still reported.

## Verified

Before:

```
zero trials RAISED ZeroDivisionError division by zero
bogus criterion echoed: something_else
run() RAISED RuntimeError TIR boom | accumulated results kept: 1
```

After:

```
zero/neg trials 0 -> ValueError: num_trials must be positive, got 0
bogus criterion   -> ValueError: Unsupported criterion 'something_else'
trace failure     -> run survived. results: 5 yield: 0.0 failed trials: 4
```

## Tests

12 tests, **9 fail without the change** — including one asserting results are *never* vacuously perfect, since that is the dangerous direction for a yield number.

title: `diffraction.py` plotting skips the matplotlib guard set up 300 lines earlier
body:
**File:** `src/diffraction.py:103-109` (sets the flag) vs `:397, 441, 468, 498, 524` (uses `plt`)

```python
103: try:
104:     import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
106:     MATPLOTLIB_AVAILABLE = True
...
397: plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))      # in plot_airy_disk — flag never consulted
```

Every other reviewed module guards (`polarization.py:346, 410`). Without matplotlib these five
methods raise `NameError: name 'plt' is not defined`, violating the AGENTS.md graceful-degradation rule.

**Fix:** add `if not MATPLOTLIB_AVAILABLE: logger.warning(...); return` at the top of each `plot_*`,
matching `PolarizationCalculator.plot_fresnel_curves`.

nodes.title: fix(diffraction): honour the matplotlib flag in all three plot methods
nodes.body:
Closes #355

## Problem

`diffraction.py` sets the flag at import:

```python
try:
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
    MATPLOTLIB_AVAILABLE = True
except ImportError:
    MATPLOTLIB_AVAILABLE = False
```

…but **never consulted it**. `plot_airy_disk`, `plot_psf_2d` and `plot_encircled_energy` went straight to `plt.figure` / `plt.subplots`, so without matplotlib all three raised:

```
NameError: name 'plt' is not defined
```

That violates the AGENTS.md rule that the app must run its core features without optional dependencies. Every other reviewed module guards — `PolarizationCalculator.plot_fresnel_curves` checks `HAS_MATPLOTLIB` — so this file was the outlier.

## Fix

Each of the three warns and returns, matching that precedent. The guard sits after the cheap scalar setup and before the first `plt` call, so a caller that only wants the numbers gets a warning-free path.

Verified by blocking matplotlib via `sys.meta_path` in a subprocess:

```
plot_airy_disk         -> returned cleanly
plot_psf_2d            -> returned cleanly
plot_encircled_energy  -> returned cleanly
non-plot maths still works: airy radius = 1.342
```

## Tests

8 tests, **2 fail without the change**: the plot methods raising, and a reflection-based check that *every* `plot_*` on the class consults the flag — so a fourth method added later cannot silently regress. Three others pass either way by design (the subprocess harness itself, the flag value, and the normal-matplotlib path), and one asserts the numerical API still works without matplotlib.

title: Two preset modules share a public name with incompatible semantics
body:
**Files:** `src/preset_library.py:252-260` vs `src/preset_lenses.py:282-284`

```python
# preset_library.py                        # preset_lenses.py
def get_preset_library() -> PresetLibrary: def get_preset_library() -> PresetLensLibrary:
    global _preset_library                  return PresetLensLibrary()
    if _preset_library is None: ...
```

Same name, same intent; one is a singleton, the other a factory. `import_custom_preset` on the factory
version is a no-op — the imported preset is discarded on the next call. `search_presets` returns
`List[LensPreset]` in one and `Dict[str, Dict]` in the other, matching on different fields. The two
test suites encode contradictory contracts (`test_preset_performance_functional.py:28` asserts the
singleton; `test_preset_lenses.py:149` uses the factory).

They also disagree on the flat-surface convention: `preset_library.py:62` uses
`radius_of_curvature_2=1e10` while `preset_lenses.py:26` uses `float("inf")`. Verified
`validate_radius(1e10)` → `ValidationError: radius magnitude must be at most 10000.0 mm`
(`MAX_RADIUS_OF_CURVATURE = 10000`), so the `preset_library` value is outside the model's own valid range.

**Fix:** delete one module (neither is wired into the GUI today) and route the survivor through
`Lens.to_dict/from_dict`.

nodes.title: refactor(preset): retire the duplicate preset module, keep the catalogue
nodes.body:
Closes #356

## Problem

Two modules exported `get_preset_library()` — same name, same intent, opposite shapes:

| | `preset_library` | `preset_lenses` |
|---|---|---|
| class | `PresetLibrary` | `PresetLensLibrary` |
| factory | **singleton** | fresh instance each call |
| `search_presets` | `List[LensPreset]` | `Dict[str, Dict]` |

`import_custom_preset` on the factory version was a **no-op** — the imported preset was discarded on the next call. The two suites encoded contradictory contracts: `test_preset_performance_functional.py` asserted the singleton while `test_preset_lenses.py` used the factory. Neither module was wired into the GUI.

## I did not just delete one

Plain deletion would have **lost content**: `preset_lenses.py` carried 14 presets against 9, and 7 categories against none — including the Edmund and Thorlabs catalogue part numbers.

`preset_library.py` is the survivor (singleton, typed `LensPreset`, category listing, and `get_lens_copy`'s `to_dict`/`from_dict` round-trip — the hand-rolled copy had drifted and dropped coatings, model-glass settings, parabolic sags and Fresnel grooves).

So its eight genuinely distinct entries are **migrated in**, optical data verbatim: Symmetric Biconvex, Kellner Eyepiece, 4x Microscope Objective, Telescope Objective, Beam Expander Element, and the three industry-standard lenses. `applications` → `typical_use`, `vendor` → `manufacturer`.

**17 presets across 9 coherent categories** — migrated entries were renamed onto the survivor's existing category labels so no subject is split across two.

## The flat-surface marker was a live bug, not a style matter

The issue framed `1e10` vs `inf` as a convention disagreement. It's worse — `lens._is_flat` is:

```python
abs(r) > LARGE_NUMBER      # strict
```

So the `1e10` this module wrote sat **exactly on the boundary**: the plano-convex preset's second surface was flat to the eye and *curved* to every code path branching on `_is_flat`. It now uses a named `FLAT_RADIUS`, and all four flat presets are correctly detected.

`validate_radius` cannot express "flat" at all — it caps `|r|` at 10000 mm *and* rejects non-finite values, so no flat radius satisfies it. That's a separate inconsistency in validation; it's recorded in the `FLAT_RADIUS` docstring and pinned by a test rather than papered over here.

## Not ported

`export_preset`, `import_custom_preset` and `get_preset_summary` lived only on the retired module. Nothing used them, so they're gone rather than reimplemented — flagging in case you want them.

## Tests

`tests/test_preset_lenses.py` tested the deleted module's dict API. Replaced by `tests/test_preset_catalogue.py` (28 tests), preserving the valuable coverage — catalogue presence, required fields, physical-validity sweep, `to_dict` round-trip, search — and adding regression tests that the retired module cannot be imported, that exactly **one** preset module defines `get_preset_library`, that migrated optical values match, and that `_is_flat` is a strict inequality.

title: `PresetLibrary.get_lens_copy` silently drops half the lens model
body:
**File:** `src/preset_library.py:226-248`

A hand-rolled field copy has drifted from `Lens.to_dict()`. Verified **not** copied:
`coating_1`, `coating_2`, `model_glass_mode`, `model_nd`, `model_vd`, `is_parabolic_1/2`,
`parabolic_sag_1/2`, `is_fresnel`, `groove_pitch`, `num_grooves`. Instantiating a preset silently
produces a different lens than the one described.

**Fix:** `d = preset.lens.to_dict(); d["id"] = uuid.uuid4().hex; ...; return Lens.from_dict(d)`.

nodes.title: fix(preset): copy the whole lens model out of a preset
nodes.body:
Closes #357

## Problem

`get_lens_copy` re-listed the `Lens` constructor fields by hand and had drifted from `Lens.to_dict()`. Twelve fields were silently dropped:

`coating_1`, `coating_2`, `model_glass_mode`, `model_nd`, `model_vd`, `is_parabolic_1/2`, `parabolic_sag_1/2`, `is_fresnel`, `groove_pitch`, `num_grooves`

Instantiating a preset produced a **different lens than the one described** — a Fresnel lens came back plano, coatings vanished, and a model glass reverted to its defaults.

```
field              original                     copy
coating_1          {'name': 'MgF2', ...}        None                <-- LOST
model_glass_mode   True                         False               <-- LOST
is_parabolic_1     True                         False               <-- LOST
is_fresnel         True                         False               <-- LOST
groove_pitch       2.5                          5.0                 <-- LOST
num_grooves        8                            None                <-- LOST
```

## Fix

Round-trip through `to_dict()`/`from_dict()` with a fresh `uuid` for the id, so the copy **cannot drift from the model again** when a field is added — the root cause was the hand-rolled duplicate list, not the missing fields.

## Tests

6 tests in `tests/test_preset_performance_functional.py`. One walks **every shipped preset** and requires an exact `to_dict()` match — all nine failed before this change, so the drift was not limited to exotic configurations.

title: `ZemaxSystemImporter` builds lenses from an untrusted file with no validation
body:
**File:** `src/export_formats.py:796-807`

```python
lens = Lens(..., thickness=pending_front["thickness"],
            diameter=surf.get("diam") or pending_front.get("ca1") or 25.0,
            clear_aperture_1=pending_front.get("ca1"), ...)
```

Verified by importing a hand-written `.zmx` with `DISZ -5.0` and `DIAM 999.0` on a 1 mm lens:
```
imported thickness: -5.0   CA1: 999.0   diameter: 1.0   CA1>diameter: True
validate_lens_parameters -> ValidationError: thickness must be positive
```

The import "succeeds" and injects a physically impossible element into the library. Same for
`preset_lenses.py:249-257`, which stores arbitrary JSON (including a non-dict) straight into
`self.presets`, after which `get_preset_summary`'s `preset['name']` raises `TypeError`.

**Fix:** run `validate_lens_parameters` / `validate_clear_aperture` per element and skip with a
warning on failure; validate the JSON shape in `import_custom_preset`.

nodes.title: fix(io): validate elements and presets read from untrusted files
nodes.body:
Closes #358

A `.zmx` file and a preset JSON are both untrusted input, and both were
being trusted straight into the live model.

## ZemaxSystemImporter

`import_system` built a `Lens` directly from whatever the file contained.
Reproduced with a hand-written `.zmx`:

```
imported thickness: -5.0   CA1: 999.0   diameter: 1.0   CA1>diameter: True
validate_lens_parameters -> ValidationError: thickness must be positive
```

Each element now goes through `validate_lens_parameters` and
`validate_clear_aperture`. An element that fails is skipped with a
warning and the import continues, so one bad element no longer discards
the rest of the system:

```
WARNING Zemax import: element 1 dropped: thickness must be positive
WARNING Zemax import: element 1 dropped, front clear aperture (999.000 mm) exceeds diameter (1.000 mm)
```

One subtlety worth noting: `validate_radius` rejects `inf`, because a
literal `0` is normally an upstream mistake. But a `.zmx` `CURV 0.0` is a
legitimate plano surface, and the `Lens` setters map `0` to `inf`.
Validating the radius literally would have rejected every plano lens in
every file, so infinite radii are probed with `MAX_RADIUS_OF_CURVATURE`.

## PresetLensLibrary

`import_custom_preset` stored whatever JSON it read into `self.presets`,
including a non-dict. `get_preset_summary` then raised `TypeError` on
`preset['name']` — deep in the GUI, far from the import that caused it.
It now rejects a non-object payload, a missing required field, and
non-string/non-numeric fields with a `ValidationError` naming the field.

## Tests

11 new tests in `tests/test_zemax_roundtrip.py`, covering negative
thickness, CA exceeding diameter, non-positive diameter, a bad element
not taking a good one with it, plano surfaces still importing, and each
preset rejection path plus a valid preset still importing.

Full suite: 1073 tests, 31 skipped, no new failures. The 6
`tests.gui_flows` loader errors are pre-existing and only occur under
`unittest` on a machine without pytest; CI runs them with pytest.

title: File > Export to STEP always fails with NameError (StepExporter typo)
body:
**Where:** `openlens.py:37` imports `StepExporter`, `openlens.py:917` calls `STEPExporter(system)`.

The call raises `NameError`, which the broad `except Exception` at `openlens.py:923` catches. The user sees "Failed to export STEP: name 'STEPExporter' is not defined", so STEP export from the GUI can never succeed.

**Repro:** `hasattr(openlens, 'STEPExporter')` is `False` and `hasattr(openlens, 'StepExporter')` is `True`.

**Fix:** use `StepExporter`. Add a smoke test that runs `_on_export_step` with a patched file dialog. The exporter itself is tested, but the GUI wiring is not.

nodes.title: fix(gui): call the STEP exporter under the name it is imported as
nodes.body:
## Description

fix(gui): call the STEP exporter under the name it is imported as

`openlens.py` imports `StepExporter` but `_on_export_step` constructed
`STEPExporter(system)`. The resulting `NameError` was swallowed by the broad
`except Exception` wrapping the export, so **File > Export to STEP could never
succeed** — the user only ever saw:

```
Failed to export STEP: name 'STEPExporter' is not defined
```

The feature had never worked. `StepExporter` itself is well covered; its GUI
wiring was not, which is why a name that is simply not bound in the module went
unnoticed.

`tests/test_gui_export_wiring.py` drives `_on_export_step` end to end through a
patched file dialog and asserts a non-empty Part 21 file appears and no error
dialog is raised. It also pins the name mismatch directly, so re-introducing a
typo fails the test rather than silently restoring a broken menu action.

### Why the typo survived

CI's `black` and `flake8` invocations only cover `src/` and `tests/`:

```yaml
run: black --line-length=100 src/ tests/ --check
run: flake8 src/ tests/ --max-line-length=100 --ignore=E203,W503 --exit-zero
```

`openlens.py` — the 50k-line GUI entry point — is therefore never linted, so an
unbound name is invisible to CI. A `pyflakes` pass over the file after the fix
reports no remaining undefined names, so this was the only instance. Widening
the lint scope to cover the entry point is a separate concern from this fix and
is deliberately left out of it.

Closes #427

      `AssertionError: [('critical', 'Export Error', "Failed to export STEP: name 'STEPExporter' is not defined")] != []`
- [x] `python3 -m unittest tests.test_gui_export_wiring` — 3 tests, OK

      six pre-existing `tests/gui_flows/test_*` loader errors that exist on clean
      `master` (they need `pytest`, which is not installed in the dev container),
      no new failures
- [x] `python3 -m pyflakes openlens.py` reports no undefined names remaining

title: Delete key shortcut deletes the current lens without confirmation (e.g. when a table has focus)
body:
**Where:** `openlens.py:540` binds "Delete Lens" to the bare `Delete` key at window level. The handler is `_on_delete_lens` at `openlens.py:652-711`.

Text fields consume Delete, but tables and lists don't. With focus in the tolerance table or an assembly list, pressing Delete removes the current lens from memory and the database. There is no confirmation and no undo. The startup dialog's delete does ask for confirmation.

**Repro (offscreen):** focus a `QTableWidget`, send Delete, and the lens count goes from 2 to 1.

**Fix:**
- Use `Ctrl+Delete`, or restrict the shortcut's context.
- Add a `QMessageBox.question` confirmation, as `startup.py:398` does.
- Longer term, add undo (see the undo/redo issue).

nodes.title: fix(gui): make deleting a lens deliberate instead of a stray keystroke
nodes.body:
## Description

fix(gui): make deleting a lens deliberate instead of a stray keystroke

`Edit > Delete Lens` was bound to the bare `Delete` key at window level and
deleted without asking. Text fields consume that key, but tables and lists do
not, so with focus in the tolerance table or an assembly list a single
keystroke removed the current lens **from memory and the database**, with no
confirmation and no undo. The startup dialog's delete already asked first; this
path did not.

Two changes:

- Bind the shortcut to `Ctrl+Delete`, so a table or list keeps the `Delete` key
  for its own use.
- Add a confirmation on the action, matching the startup dialog and
  **defaulting to `No`**, so a stray `Enter` cannot mean delete.

The prompt sits on the action rather than inside `_on_delete_lens`, so
programmatic callers keep deleting without a modal dialog and `_on_delete_lens`
stays the single place that decides what is refusable. `_deletable_item()`
shares the last-lens rule so the prompt never asks about a deletion that would
be refused the moment after.

Also corrects the `Keyboard Shortcuts` help, which still advertised the old
`Delete` binding.

### Why the tests do not send a synthetic key event

These assert the action's shortcut sequence and the slot's behaviour rather
than posting a `Delete` key to a focused table. An offscreen window is never
activated, so window-level shortcuts never fire at all — such a test passes
whether or not the shortcut is bound to `Delete`, i.e. a green test proving
nothing. Driving the slot directly also keeps the assertion independent of Qt's
keyboard routing, which is not what regressed here.

- [x] Bug fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)

## Related Issues

Closes #428

- [x] Added a regression test that fails before this change and passes after —
      confirmed, the pre-fix run produced 1 failure + 5 errors, including
      `AssertionError: 'Del' unexpectedly ... Delete Lens is still bound to the bare Delete key`
- [x] `python3 -m unittest tests.test_gui_delete_shortcut` — 6 tests, OK
- [x] `python3 -m unittest tests.test_gui_export_wiring tests.test_deletion_persistence tests.test_lens_menu tests.test_gui` — 58 tests, OK (the 7 pre-existing `_on_delete_lens` call sites are untouched)
- [x] `black --line-length=100 src/ tests/ --check` — 210 files unchanged

- [ ] Full local suite — 1585 tests, same six pre-existing
      `tests/gui_flows/test_*` loader errors (they need `pytest`, unavailable in
      the dev container), no new failures
